title: Common mistakes that sink design rounds
scopeHtml: Scope: eight frequent mistakes and how to fix them. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Mistake 1: designing before clarifying
notes.html:
The most common failure is solving a problem nobody asked. Without scope, you build chat with video calls, search, payments and end-to-end encryption, then run out of time with nothing deep.

Fix: spend the first 3 to 5 minutes on 3 to 5 sharp questions, then repeat the scope back: "so we support 1:1 and group text, delivery receipts, no media, 50M DAU, correct?"

Worked example. "Design YouTube" can mean upload and transcoding, playback streaming, search, recommendations or comments. Each is a different system. If you pick "upload plus playback, 100M DAU, no recommendations", you can reach real depth (transcoding pipeline, CDN) in 45 minutes.

Industry examples. Real design docs at Google and Amazon list "non-goals" explicitly for the same reason; unbounded scope kills projects.

Decision gravity. Scope is reversible in the room (the interviewer can widen it) but each added feature adds boxes, so be deliberate.

Everyday analogy. Ordering food: "what do you feel like?" before the waiter starts cooking.

Common interview traps.

  • Asking 15 questions with no effect on the design.
  • Never stating assumptions, so the interviewer cannot correct you early.

notes.title: Mistake 2: no numbers
notes.html:
A design without numbers cannot be judged. "We'll use a cache" is meaningless without how big, how many requests, what hit ratio.

Fix: do the estimation (see F3), and attach a number to every major decision: cache size, shard count, partition count, replica count, TTL.

Worked example. "Peak 70K reads/s; cache absorbs 95%, leaving 3.5K reads/s for Postgres, one primary and two replicas are enough. 200 writes/s fits one primary. So no sharding yet." That one paragraph shows you can be trusted with capacity decisions.

Industry examples. Capacity reviews at Netflix, Uber and Stripe start from QPS, latency percentile and storage growth; numbers are the common language between teams.

Everyday analogy. A recipe without quantities.

Common interview traps.

  • Numbers at the start, then forgotten when choosing components.
  • Wildly wrong orders of magnitude (off by 1000x) that go unnoticed.

notes.title: Mistake 3: buzzword stacking and over-engineering
notes.html:
Kafka, Redis, Cassandra, Kubernetes, microservices, all by minute five. More boxes means more failure modes and more cost. Senior engineers are valued for choosing the simplest design that meets the numbers.

Fix: start with a monolith-ish stateless tier plus a relational DB. Add a component only when a requirement or number demands it, and say which one.

Worked example. 200 writes/s and 5 TB of data: a single Postgres with replicas handles it. Proposing Cassandra plus Kafka plus Elasticsearch adds three systems to run for no gain. At 200K writes/s, 500 TB, the story changes.

Industry examples. Stack Overflow ran on a few SQL Server machines; Instagram's early stack was Django, Postgres, Redis, memcached. Shopify scaled a Rails monolith for years with sharded MySQL (pods). Segment and Amazon Prime Video have publicly written about moving from microservices back to a monolith for cost and simplicity.

Decision gravity. Microservices are a near one-way door: splitting is easy, merging back is painful and distributed transactions cost you consistency. Start modular and split on team or scaling pressure.

Everyday analogy. Buying a truck to carry a loaf of bread.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming a technology without saying what it replaces or why.
  • Choosing a NoSQL database "for scale" when the data is relational and small.

notes.title: Mistake 4: ignoring failure and edge cases
notes.html:
Designs that assume everything works are mid-level. The senior signal is to describe what happens when it does not: node crash, network partition, duplicate message, retry storm, slow dependency, hot key.

Fix: for each component ask four questions: what if it is down, slow, wrong, or overloaded? Mention timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, idempotency keys, circuit breakers, dead-letter queues.

Worked example. Payment call times out. Did it succeed? Retrying could double-charge. Answer: client sends an idempotency key, server stores key and result for 24 h; a retry with the same key returns the stored result. Stripe's API works exactly this way.

Industry examples. AWS's 2017 S3 outage (a typo in a command removed too many servers) and Facebook's October 2021 BGP outage are standard case studies in cascading failure and missing safeguards. Netflix uses Hystrix-style circuit breakers and chaos testing.

Production symptom. Retry storm: dependency slows, clients retry, load triples, dependency dies. The metric to watch is request rate versus success rate; with retries, request rate climbs while successes fall.

Everyday analogy. Wearing a seatbelt: you do not expect to crash, you plan for it.

Common interview traps.

  • Retries without backoff, jitter or a cap.
  • Exactly-once claims; real systems do at-least-once plus idempotent handling.
  • Forgetting the load balancer, queue or cache as single points of failure.

notes.title: Mistake 5: ignoring trade-offs and consistency
notes.html:
Every choice gives something up. Saying "it has no downside" is a red flag. The classic ones: consistency vs availability, latency vs durability, cost vs speed, read vs write optimisation, simplicity vs flexibility.

Fix: use a template for each decision: "I choose X because Y; the alternative is Z, which is better when W; X breaks when V."

Worked example. Cache plus DB. Write-through keeps cache fresh but doubles write latency (say 2 ms to 5 ms); cache-aside (invalidate on write) is simpler but allows a stale read for a few milliseconds after a race. For a profile page the stale read is fine; for an account balance it is not, so read balance from the primary.

Industry examples. Amazon's Dynamo chose availability and eventual consistency for the shopping cart; Google Spanner pays commit latency (TrueTime waits, on the order of several milliseconds) to give external consistency. Both were deliberate.

Decision gravity. Consistency model is usually a one-way door because application code assumes it; weakening later breaks invariants, strengthening later costs latency and a migration.

Everyday analogy. Fast, cheap, good: pick two.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming strong consistency and high availability across partitions (CAP).
  • Not saying which data needs which consistency level.

notes.title: Mistake 6: poor communication and rigid behaviour
notes.html:
Silence, monologue, defensiveness and ignoring hints sink strong engineers. The interviewer is a collaborator who wants to see how you work in a team.

Fixes:

  • Think aloud in short sentences; summarise your plan before each phase.
  • Check in: "does this direction work, or should I go deeper elsewhere?"
  • Treat hints as free gifts: "good point, that changes X, let me revise."
  • Use the whiteboard tidily: left to right data flow, label arrows, number the steps.

Worked example. Interviewer: "what if one user has 50M followers?" Weak: "that won't happen." Strong: "that breaks fan-out on write, since a post costs 50M writes. I would switch celebrities to fan-out on read and merge at read time. Thanks, that also affects the cache size."

Industry examples. Hiring rubrics at large companies score collaboration separately (often called communication or "working with the interviewer") because design work in real life is a team activity: design reviews, RFCs, incident calls.

Everyday analogy. Pair driving: the navigator helps; arguing about the route wastes time.

Common interview traps.

  • Arguing with feedback instead of exploring it.
  • Reading from a memorised script and not noticing the interviewer is lost.
  • Not handling a mistake gracefully; admit, fix, move on.

notes.title: Mistake 7: shallow breadth, no depth; and bad time use
notes.html:
Ten boxes and no deep dive is the classic mid-level pattern. Seniors pick a hard part and go to mechanism: data structures, protocols, failure behaviour, numbers.

Fix: after the high-level design, say "I will go deep on X because it is the riskiest part". Know at least five deep topics well: sharding and rebalancing, replication and failover, caching and invalidation, queues and delivery semantics, consistency and transactions.

Worked example. Deep dive on "sharding the messages table": choose key (conversation_id, not user_id, so one chat lives on one shard), 64 logical shards on 8 physical nodes (so you can rebalance without re-hashing), hot conversation handling, cross-shard queries via a separate index. That is a full senior answer.

Industry examples. Instagram used logical shards mapped onto fewer physical Postgres servers; Pinterest sharded MySQL with a mapping table; Slack's Vitess adoption is a modern example of operating sharding at scale.

Time use. Over-long estimation or API sections starve the deep dive; keep to the timeline from F1 and say when you are skipping something on purpose.

Everyday analogy. A doctor who orders every test but diagnoses nothing.

Common interview traps.

  • Mentioning sharding but unable to say what the shard key is, or what breaks (cross-shard joins, hot shard).
  • Running out of time before covering failure and monitoring.
  • Treating the interviewer's deep question as an attack rather than an invitation.

notes.title: Mistake 8: forgetting operations, security and cost
notes.html:
Real systems must be run. Candidates who never mention monitoring, deployment, rate limiting, authentication, data privacy or cost look like they have never been on call.

Mention briefly:

  • Observability: p50/p99 latency, error rate, saturation (queue lag, connection pool), tracing IDs.
  • Rollout: canary or blue-green, feature flags, backward-compatible schema changes.
  • Security: authN/authZ, TLS, rate limiting, input validation, PII encryption.
  • Cost: biggest line (egress, storage, compute) and one lever to cut it.

Worked example. "Alert if p99 > 500 ms for 5 minutes or error rate > 1%; deploy 5% canary for 15 minutes; rate limit 100 req/min per user at the gateway; move media older than 90 days to cold storage to cut the largest cost line by roughly 60%." Concrete, short, believable.

Industry examples. Google's SRE golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) are a standard checklist. Stripe, Cloudflare and AWS publish public post-mortems that show how missing rollouts safeguards cause incidents.

Decision gravity. Observability and rollout are cheap to add early and expensive to retrofit; schema-change discipline (expand then contract) is the difference between a safe migration and an outage.

Everyday analogy. A shop needs a till, locks and a cleaning schedule, not only shelves.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaving security entirely out for a payments or health prompt.
  • Saying "we will monitor it" with no metric names.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Clarify scope first; state assumptions and non-goals.
  • Use numbers and let them drive every component choice.
  • Start simple; add components only when a number or requirement demands it.
  • Describe failure, retries, idempotency and single points of failure.
  • Name trade-offs for every decision, including consistency level and reversibility.
  • Communicate: think aloud, check in, take hints gracefully.
  • Go deep on the riskiest part; manage time; finish with operations, security and cost.
